# Migri Processing Times 2026 — Current Waits by Permit Type, Statutory Maximums and What to Do About a Delay

Migri processing times by permit type, checked 14 October 2026: work, specialist, Fast Track, student and family. When the clock starts and what to do about a delay.

Written by · Erkan Bayar Legal review · Samed Karakas, Legal Counsel Sources checked · 2026-10-14 Reading time · 13 min

## Short answer

Checked against Migri on 14 October 2026: first permits for employed persons (TTOL) that ended in a positive decision took an average of 17 days in July 2026, specialists usually get a decision in about two weeks, and Fast Track for specialists, EU Blue Card holders and start-up entrepreneurs has a 14-day target. About 82% of positive decisions on first student permits come within 30 days. Family-based applications have a statutory maximum of nine months, and Migri has reported backlogs in them. The clock starts when you prove your identity, not when you submit, and the card takes about two more weeks after the decision. Migri publishes two estimates per application type — most cases and a minority of cases — and if yours has not been taken up within the shorter one, the longer applies. Statutory maximums are a separate thing: two months for work-based permits, three for studies and nine for family ties. If you applied for an extension before the old permit expired, you may keep working while you wait. Migri asks you not to call when an estimate is exceeded; if a statutory maximum is exceeded, a free complaint to the Parliamentary Ombudsman is possible, but the Ombudsman cannot change a decision.

## The tool for this

- Migri fees 2026: what each application costs The fee for this application, online and on paper, and when it is not refunded.
- Which documents do you need? The checklist for this application, with what has to be translated or legalised.

## 1. Current Migri processing times by permit type

The table collects what Migri itself was reporting when we checked on 14 October 2026, next to the time limit set by law or by Migri's own service target. Migri states its figures in different forms for different permits — an average for one, a most-cases estimate for another, the share decided within a month for a third — and the table keeps each figure in the form Migri used rather than turning them into a single number Migri never published.

None of these is a promise for your application. Migri updates its estimates every two months and the averages for employed persons every month, so before you fix a start date or book a flight, open Migri's processing-times page or its processing-time checker, choose your exact application type and read the current figure there. Where we could not verify a current figure from Migri for a permit type, the table says so instead of guessing.

| Application | What Migri reports | Limit in law or service target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Employed person (TTOL), first permit | Most cases one month, a minority two months; positive decisions averaged 17 days in July 2026 | Two months in law, counted from the biometrics visit; Migri's own goal is one month |
| Employed person (TTOL), extended permit | Averages for July 2026: 37 days for positive decisions, 162 days for refusals | Two months in law |
| Specialist | About two weeks in most cases, up to two months in a minority | Two months in law; Fast Track target 14 days for a first permit |
| EU Blue Card | First permits can go through Fast Track; for extensions, read the live estimate | Two months in law; Fast Track target 14 days for a first permit |
| Start-up entrepreneur | Can go through Fast Track once Business Finland has issued its statement | Fast Track target 14 days |
| Studies, first permit | About 82% of positive decisions within 30 days; with no decision by then, Migri's estimate is 90 days | Three months in law |
| Family ties, first permit | Migri has reported backlogs; read the live estimate for your exact family category | Nine months in law; 90 days for a student's family member when no additional information is needed |
| Permanent residence permit | No figure verified; read the live estimate. The requirements changed on 8 January 2026 | No general maximum in law; six months for the EU long-term resident's permit |
| Finnish citizenship | Migri has reported a backlog that it is clearing; read the live estimate | No general maximum in law; 12 months for persons under protection |
| EU citizen, registration of right of residence | Listed under EU citizens in Migri's table; read the live estimate | Six months for the residence card of an EU citizen's family member |

## 2. When the clock starts and when it stops

The most common misunderstanding is that the clock starts the moment you submit. According to Migri the processing time starts when you have proved your identity, which happens at a service point visit or, for some online applications, on submission in Enter Finland. The time ends when the decision is ready.

The card has to be counted in as well. After the decision, producing and posting the residence permit card takes about two more weeks. "The decision is out" and "the card is in my hand" are therefore not the same day, and travel or a starting date at work should be planned around the card.

For work-based permits the Aliens Act says this in so many words: the decision is due within two months of the authority receiving a properly completed application with its attachments, and the time is counted from the visit at which you give your fingerprints and other biometrics — at a Finnish mission or an external service provider abroad, or at a Migri service point in Finland. Migri also says it can start on an employed person's application before identity has been proved, and that an employer who submits the terms of employment without delay speeds the processing up.

## 3. Two estimates and how to read them

For each application type Migri publishes not one time but two estimates: the processing time in most cases and the processing time in a minority of cases. The rule is plain: if your application has not been taken up during the shorter estimate, the longer estimate in the table is the one that applies in your case.

The estimates are based on how long most decisions took in the preceding months and how many similar applications arrived in the past two months; they are updated every two months. The time spent in the queue is included in the estimate. If no additional information has to be requested, the shorter estimate will most likely apply.

For one application rather than a whole permit type, Migri's processing-time checker is the more precise tool. It is built on the same statistics, so it will not move your application forward, but it is the quickest way to see the estimate that applies to your own case rather than to the average applicant.

## 4. Maximum times laid down by law

Alongside the estimate there is also a maximum time laid down by law, and the two should not be confused. The estimate is a statistic; the statutory time is an obligation. Migri's tables show separately which applications have a maximum time provided by law, and not every application has one.

### Checklist

- Residence permits on the basis of work: 2 months, counted from the visit at which biometrics are given
- Residence permit on the basis of studies: 3 months
- Residence permit on the basis of family ties: 9 months
- A student's family member: 90 days from a complete application
- Residence card of an EU citizen's family member: 6 months
- EU long-term resident's residence permit: 6 months
- Citizenship application of persons under protection: 12 months
- Asylum: 18 months where the investigation requires it, and 21 months where the situation in the country of departure is unstable

## 5. Why applications are delayed

Migri lists the reasons for delay on its own page: the number of requirements that have to be investigated, the number of applications arriving for the same permit type, whether automation can be used, and the maximum times prescribed by law. The time spent waiting in the queue belongs to this picture too.

The single most common cause is a request for additional information. If a piece of information or an attachment is missing, Migri asks you for the document and the processing waits for it to arrive. Being invited to an interview, an unpaid processing fee, a requirement that is not met, or a request for an exception all lengthen the time as well. If your application is waiting for information from another authority — an interview at a Finnish mission, for example — Migri cannot influence that authority's waiting times.

## 6. The right to work while you wait

For an employee waiting on an extension there is one decisive date. If you applied for the extended permit before your current permit expired, you may go on working in accordance with that permit while the decision is awaited. If you applied only after the previous permit had expired, you are not allowed to continue working on the basis of the old permit.

There are exceptions. In seasonal work, continuing depends on your going on working for the same employer; with au pair, working holiday and intra-corporate transfer (ICT) permits the right to work ends when the permit ends. An employer may ask the employee to show the residence permit card and a document about the pending application; that document is Migri's certificate of a pending application.

## 7. Migri asks you not to call — so what does help

Migri's wording is plain: you do not need to contact it if the estimate has been exceeded. An automated message is sent when the processing situation of your application changes, an online applicant sees the status in their Enter Finland account, and Migri will contact you if it needs additional information. Customer service cannot give exact details about the processing of your application.

What actually helps is removing in advance the reasons that lengthen the time: applying when you already meet the requirements, applying online through Enter Finland, filling in every section of the form carefully and adding all the required attachments, and paying the processing fee in Enter Finland before you submit. Once these are in order Migri can usually use automation, and the decision comes faster.

There is one formal right alongside Migri's request. Under section 23 of the Administrative Procedure Act (hallintolaki) a matter must be dealt with without undue delay, and the authority must, if the party asks, give an estimate of when the decision will be issued and answer enquiries about how the processing is progressing. When you have a concrete reason — a job with a start date, a lease, a family event — a short written request that cites that section is a legitimate way to get an answer, and far more useful than calling the helpline again.

## 8. When a statutory time is exceeded: complaint options

Exceeding the estimate and exceeding the statutory maximum do not weigh the same. Where the second has happened, a complaint can be made to the Parliamentary Ombudsman (eduskunnan oikeusasiamies). Undue delay in dealing with a matter is expressly among the things the Ombudsman investigates; the complaint is free, and a person may complain on their own, together with others, or on someone else's behalf.

The limits are worth knowing too. The Ombudsman cannot amend or overturn decisions made by authorities; to obtain a change, the legal means of appeal provided by law must be used. As a rule the Ombudsman does not investigate a matter pending before another authority, but delay in the processing is the exception to that rule. A complaint concerning a matter older than two years is not investigated unless there are special reasons.

# How EU/EEA Citizens Register Their Right of Residence in Finland

 By Finland Handbook Editorial Team July 8, 2026 October 28, 2026 October 28, 2026 

Moving to Finland as an EU/EEA citizen often feels like a straightforward step, but the reality of administrative processes can quickly introduce layers of confusion that many expats encounter. While you might not need a residence permit in the traditional sense, you absolutely need to register your right of residence if you plan to stay longer than three months, and missing this crucial step can cause unnecessary headaches down the line. This guide will walk you through everything you need to know to navigate this initial but vital bureaucratic hurdle, ensuring a smooth start to your Finnish adventure.

Table of Contents

## Understanding Your EU/EEA Right of Residence in Finland

When you're an EU/EEA citizen, the concept of "residence rights" can feel a bit nebulous, especially when you're used to the freedom of movement within the Schengen area. You've heard that you don't need a visa or a residence permit, and that's generally true – but it doesn't mean you can just waltz in and stay indefinitely without telling anyone. Finland, like all other EU countries, requires you to officially register your presence if your stay extends beyond a short tourist visit.

### What "Right of Residence" Really Means for EU/EEA Citizens

For us EU/EEA folks, "right of residence" isn't about asking permission to live here, it's about informing the authorities that you are exercising your existing right to do so. Think of it less as an application and more as a declaration. Unlike third-country nationals who must apply for a visa or a proper residence permit, our status is protected by EU law. This means you have the fundamental right to live, work, study, or retire in any EU/EEA member state, including Finland, without needing prior authorization.

However, this doesn't exempt you from all administrative obligations. The moment you decide to make Finland your home for more than 90 days, you trigger a requirement to let the Finnish Immigration Service (Migri) know. This registration is absolutely crucial because it's the first official step in integrating into the Finnish system. Without it, you might find yourself in a bureaucratic limbo, unable to access public services or even open a bank account easily. It's a common point of frustration for many newcomers; you think you're "home free" as an EU citizen, but then you hit this wall of registration, proving you have a solid reason to be here.

### The Legal Basis: EU Law and Finnish Implementation

The framework for your right of residence comes directly from EU law, specifically Directive 2004/38/EC, which outlines the rights of EU citizens and their family members to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States. Finland, as an EU member, has incorporated this directive into its national legislation, mainly through the Aliens Act (Ulkomaalaislaki).

This legislation stipulates that if an EU/EEA citizen intends to stay in Finland for longer than three months, they must register their right of residence with the Finnish Immigration Service, Migri. This three-month period starts from your arrival date. The whole point of this system is to ensure that while you have the freedom to move, the host country still has a clear record of who is residing within its borders and under what conditions. It's about maintaining public order, security, and ensuring that individuals have legitimate means of support. So, while it's not a "permit," it carries similar weight in terms of getting you into the official system. Ignoring this requirement can lead to issues later on, such as difficulties with employment, social benefits, or even facing a fine or removal from the country if you're found to be residing illegally after the initial three months. You might wonder, "Do EU Citizens Need a Residence Permit to Live in Finland?" The answer is no, but you do need this essential registration, which this guide details further.

## When and Where to Register Your Stay

Navigating the timeline and the correct authority for registration can feel like a puzzle when you first arrive. It's one of those things where timing is everything, and knowing where to go can save you a world of hassle.

### The Three-Month Window: Don't Delay!

Let me tell you, as someone who's seen it all, the three-month rule is etched in stone. You have exactly three months from the date you enter Finland to register your right of residence with Migri. It sounds generous, but those initial weeks fly by faster than you can say "terveyskeskus." You're busy finding an apartment, maybe starting a new job, learning a few Finnish phrases, and suddenly you realize you're nearing the deadline.

What happens if you miss it? Well, it's not the end of the world, but it can definitely complicate things. Migri might ask for an explanation for the delay, and while they usually process late applications, it adds an unnecessary layer of stress and potential scrutiny. More importantly, until you're registered, you're essentially in a grey area. You might struggle to open a bank account, get an official tax card, or access certain social services. It’s like trying to run a race without a bib number – technically possible, but you won't be officially recognized. Trust me, get it done within that window. Set a reminder in your phone, mark it on your calendar, whatever it takes.

### The Finnish Immigration Service (Migri): Your Registration Hub

So, where do you actually go to do this? The official body responsible for processing registrations for EU/EEA citizens is the Finnish Immigration Service, or Migri (Maahanmuuttovirasto). They handle all things related to immigration, from residence permits for non-EU citizens to the registration of EU nationals.

The good news is that Migri has streamlined a lot of its processes through their online service, Enter Finland. This is going to be your primary portal for almost everything immigration-related in Finland. You initiate your registration application through the Enter Finland website. It's a fairly user-friendly platform, but it does require attention to detail, so make sure you have all your documents ready before you start.

After you've submitted your application online, the next crucial step is to book an appointment at a Migri service point for identification. This is where you'll present your original documents, prove your identity, and sometimes provide biometrics (though for EU registration, it's mostly about verifying your identity and documents). You can find the nearest Migri service point on their website, usually in major cities like Helsinki, Tampere, Turku, or Oulu. Remember to book this appointment as soon as you submit your online application, because appointment slots, especially in busy periods, can fill up fast! This whole process of interacting with the system is covered in more detail in our guide on Dealing with Migri and Enter Finland: Applications, Waiting, and Decisions.

## The Essential Requirements for Registration

When you're registering your right of residence, Migri isn't just looking for a heartbeat; they want to see that you have a legitimate reason to be in Finland and that you won't become an undue burden on the social welfare system. This means you need to demonstrate a basis for your stay, whether it's through work, study, family, or simply having enough funds to support yourself.

### Proving Your Basis of Residence: Work, Study, Family, or Sufficient Funds

This is the core of your application. You need to clearly show Migri why you're here. Each category has its own set of requirements, so make sure you pick the one that best describes your situation.

#### Employment

If you've landed a job in Finland, fantastic! This is one of the most common and straightforward ways to register. You'll need to provide evidence of your employment. This typically means:

- An employment contract: A valid, signed contract from a Finnish employer.
- Proof of salary/income: This could be your first payslip, a certificate from your employer stating your monthly salary, or bank statements showing regular income deposits.

Migri needs to see that you have stable employment that allows you to support yourself. The job doesn't have to be full-time, but it should be sufficient to meet your living costs. Finland values self-sufficiency, and a job is a clear indicator of that. For a deeper dive into finding and securing employment, check out our comprehensive guide, Working in Finland as a Foreigner: The Complete Guide (2027).

#### Self-Employment

Thinking of starting your own business or working as a freelancer? That's also a valid basis! For self-employed individuals, you'll need to show that your business is legitimate and generates enough income. This could include:

- Business registration documents: Proof that your company (e.g., toiminimi or osakeyhtiö) is registered in Finland.
- Business plan: A brief outline of your business activities and financial projections can be helpful.
- Proof of income/financial solvency: Bank statements, invoices, or a professional accounting statement showing that you have sufficient funds to support yourself through your entrepreneurial activities.

It’s about demonstrating viability. Migri wants to be sure your venture is genuinely capable of sustaining you.

#### Study

Finland is a fantastic place to study, and if you're here as a student, your registration process is generally smooth. You will need:

- Acceptance letter from a Finnish educational institution: This proves your enrollment in a recognized course of study.
- Proof of sufficient funds: You'll need to show you have enough money to cover your living expenses for the duration of your studies. While exact amounts can vary, Migri publishes guidelines, often around €560 per month. This could be demonstrated through bank statements, scholarship letters, or a sponsor's undertaking.
- Health insurance: If your studies don't automatically grant you access to public healthcare (e.g., if you're not in the population register yet or not working), you might need to show proof of comprehensive private health insurance.

Make sure your study program is recognized and that you're prepared to show financial stability. More on student life and permits can be found in Studying in Finland: A Complete Guide for International Students (2027).

#### Family Ties

Are you moving to Finland to join a spouse, registered partner, or a close family member who is already residing here? This is the basis for family reunification. You'll typically need:

- Proof of your relationship: A marriage certificate, birth certificate, or a certificate of registered partnership.
- The family member's registration details: Your family member who is already in Finland and registered will need to provide proof of their own right of residence.
- Proof of sufficient funds (if applicable): While generally the family member's income is assessed, in some cases, you might also need to demonstrate independent financial means or comprehensive health insurance.

It's important that the family relationship is genuine and verifiable. Sometimes, official documents from outside Finland need to be translated, which is where services like RushTranslate or Translayte can be incredibly useful to ensure your marriage or birth certificates are accepted by Finnish authorities. For more on this, consult our article on Family Reunification in Finland: Bringing Your Loved Ones on a Family Permit.

#### Sufficient Funds

This category is for those who aren't working, studying, or joining family but still wish to reside in Finland. This could be retirees, individuals with passive income, or those just taking a sabbatical. You'll need to demonstrate:

- C

Anecdotal evidence suggests checking first thing in the morning (e.g., 8:00 AM EET) or late in the evening can yield results, as these might be when daily allocations are updated or when others cancel.
- Expand Your Search: If you absolutely cannot find a slot in your preferred city, consider if you can travel to another service point. For example, if you live in Helsinki, check Tampere or Turku. While it requires a train ticket, getting the appointment secured might be worth the cost and hassle compared to delays in your permit process.
- Don't Procrastinate: As soon as you submit your application via Enter Finland and get the notification that you need an appointment, start looking. Do not wait until the last minute. The earlier you start, the more chances you have.
- Understand the "Treatment Guarantee" (Hoitotakuu) Mentality: While not directly related to appointments, Finland operates with a "treatment guarantee" for healthcare, meaning you shouldn't wait endlessly for critical services. For immigration, while there isn't a strict legal guarantee for appointment times, Migri does aim to process applications within reasonable timeframes. If you've been searching for an excessively long time and are facing an imminent expiry of your current permit or visa, it might be worth contacting Migri's customer service directly to explain your situation, though this is a last resort. Keep evidence of your attempts to book.

sources.title: Residence in Finland for EU citizens: Migri and DVV | Hello Expat
highlights:
Only if you stay longer than three months. Up to three months you need nothing but a valid passport or identity card. The InfoFinland page on EU citizens specifies that the three months are counted from your last departure from Finland, not from the first time you ever visited.

Beyond three months, you apply to the Finnish Immigration Service (Maahanmuuttovirasto, Migri) to register your right of residence. The deadline, per InfoFinland, is three months from arrival. This applies to citizens of EU member states, Liechtenstein and Switzerland. Citizens of Denmark, Iceland, Norway and Sweden do not apply to Migri at all; they register their personal data at the DVV (Digi- ja väestötietovirasto, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency).

...

1. Apply in Enter Finland (the online service) or on a paper form. You must submit it yourself, although you can apply for your child.
2. Pay €53. In 2026 the fee is the same online and on paper. You can pay by card or Finnish online banking when you submit, or at the service point.
3. Book an appointment at a Migri service point to prove your identity. Bring your passport or identity card and the originals and copies of your attachments.
4. Wait for the decision. Migri may contact you for more information.
5. Collect the decision at the service point, in Enter Finland or by post. If approved, you may receive the EU registration certificate on the spot or later.

sources.title: Arrival at Aalto University | Aalto University
highlights:
EU/EEA, Switzerland and Liechtenstein citizens do not need a residence permit, instead they register their right of residence at the Finnish Immigration Service. The registration is required if you are staying in Finland for over 90 days without leaving the country. You can also obtain the Finnish personal identity code in connection with the registration.

You can fill in the online application once your study right has started and then book the appointment to visit the service point in Helsinki. The Finnish Immigration Service point in Helsinki is very busy and when you book an appointment, the next available time may be several weeks or even a few months away.

...

Students must personally cover the costs if they become ill, therefore you must have sufficient insurance that is valid for the whole duration of your stay in Finland. Please note that exchange students do not have access to Finnish Student Health Services (FSHS).

If you need to apply for the residence permit (non-EU/EEA citizens), you must take out private insurance that covers medical and drug expenses. For more information, please see Migri’s website on insurance.

EU/EEA citizens must take the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) with them to Finland. By presenting the European Health Insurance Card, you can prove the right to medically necessary treatment in Finland. The card must be valid for the whole duration of your exchange. We strongly recommend purchasing private health insurance as well, because it is significantly easier and faster to make an appointment at a private clinic.

sources.title: Moving to Finland: documents and first steps – SuomiGuide
highlights:
Enter Finland is Migri's online application service. Each application type has its own supporting-document list. Foreign documents may need translation or legalisation, so prepare them before the identification appointment.

| Document or information | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Passport or accepted identity document | Establishing identity |
| Employment contract, study place or family certificate | Supporting the selected residence grounds |
| Tenancy agreement and exact address | Arranging accommodation and address records |
| Application's attachment list | Assembling that application's documents |

Create a document list recording the original, translation and application to which each item belongs. An employment contract can then be located for both immigration and tax matters. Migri's application guidance.

highlights: If You Don't Do It: Without a registration certificate from Migri, you cannot proceed to DVV to obtain a personal identity code or municipality of residence, which in turn blocks access to Kela benefits, banking, and municipal services.
